newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico stocks inch up on follow-through, Dow.
newsitem.headline: Mexico stocks inch up on follow-through, Dow.

text.p: The Mexican bourse opened marginally up on Tuesday on what dealers said was underlying strength carried over from recent sessions bolstered by an upward Dow Jones.
"Telmex is up, and was about the only stock holding us back yesterday, even then we only closed down a couple of points, so the market is firm," a desk trader said.
The leading IPC share index was up 10.01 points, or 0.23 percent, at 4,446.76. Trading volume was moderate at 2.1 million shares.
"Trade is quiet, but firm. It's the same story, Telmex, Bancomer, Cemex and Cifra are all solid," a floor trader said.
Telecoms firm Telmex was up 6 centavos to 19.20 pesos, while its ADRs had gained 5/8 to 48-3/8. The Dow Jones was meanwhile up 60.84 points at 7,665.10.
Dealers said they awaited wider market reaction to news of a management changeover at Telmex.
One of Mexico's largest financial groups, Bancomer, gained 9 centavos to 4.01 pesos, a level not seen since February 1994, before the December 1994 devaluation crisis.
Dealers said financials were considered cheap in valuation terms by foreign investors.
Retail firm Cifra was up 10 centavos to 14.70 pesos, on what dealers said was demand ahead of a dividend payment, whose approval was expected later in the day.
Cement firm Cemex was up 60 centavos to 32.50 on what traders said was a favorable outlook for second quarter earnings for the sector, driven by strong industrial output data released last week.
Dealers said they saw limited upside potential for the bourse during the remainder of the session.
"I can't see the Dow recouping all of yesterday's losses, and I expect the market here to be slow in the run up to the elections, and the FOMC meeting," a desk trader said.
The Federal Open Market Committee meeting will meet on July 2 to review U.S. interest rate policy.

Mexico will hold mid-term elections on July 6 to renew the entire lower chamber of Congress, one-quarter of the Senate, several state governors, and will elect Mexico City's mayor for the first time in modern history.
On the broad market, of 49 stocks traded, 20 were up while nine were down.
